approach_variants.name: The North Star-Bonanza col, then talus south to the white slabs beside the caret-shaped snowpatch
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach as its neighbours and the same camp: drive to Chelan, ferry to Lucerne, bus to Holden Village, then about eleven miles of trail and cross-country to a camp near 7,000 ft at the North Star-Bonanza col. It is a full day of travel and approach before anything else happens.

From camp the base is reached over talus. This route is on the WEST FACE proper rather than the north-west buttress its two neighbours share, and it tops out just right of the Southwest Summit.

It is sixteen pitches, just over 2,000 ft of net gain and about 2,800 ft of climbing, with a great deal of loose rock and several pitches where the protection is minimal and the holds are portable. Bail options near the summit roof systems are poor.

The descent from the Southwest Summit traverses to the Isella Glacier and follows an undulating line of steep rock and moraine at about two-thirds of the glacier's height, then crosses a notch in the south ridge back to the col camp — two ropes.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Sep; the only ascent on record is late August, and its two neighbours were also climbed in late summer for the driest rock
hazards: Abundant loose rock over sixteen pitches, with several pitches on minimal protection and portable holds
Poor retreat options near the summit roof systems on a wall with no fixed gear
A descent that crosses the Isella Glacier and a notch in the south ridge, needing two ropes and daylight
Rock quality that varies pitch by pitch, including a choss band low on the route taken at 5.9R
Remoteness on the scale of a three-day weekend before the first pitch, on boat-and-bus access that is currently closed
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST PITCH BEGINS AT A SMALL CARET-SHAPED SNOWPATCH, AND YOU START JUST RIGHT OF IT. That patch is the marker the first-ascent party chose to record, and it is the only thing at the base of this wall that is a shape rather than a description. Walk the talus until you find it.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS A COLOUR CHANGE, AND IT IS EXCELLENT IN BAD LIGHT: pitch one is a 220 ft scramble at about 5.4 up WHITE SLABS to a stance below a large, steeper band of DARKER rock. White below, dark above, easy climbing. If your first pitch is hard, or if the rock is uniform, you are somewhere else.

THE SECOND CONFIRMATION IS ABOVE THE FIRST: from that stance you are aiming for an OBVIOUS, LARGE OPEN BOOK, which takes the second pitch at 5.8. A big open corner directly above easy white slabs is the pair of features that identifies this route. One without the other is not enough.

LEFT TO RIGHT ACROSS THIS WALL, FACING IT FROM THE WEST: OREGONIAN, SOVIET, CASCADIAN. This is the RIGHT-hand one — looker's right of both older routes, which are on the north-west buttress and are out of view at the far left margin of the wall from here. If you can see two other lines to your left and none to your right, you are in the correct place.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE STRONGEST ON THIS PAGE, AND IT IS ABOUT WHAT LIES FURTHER RIGHT: the part of the wall to the right of this route, above the LONG SNOWFIELD, IS UNCLIMBED, and the party who looked hardest at it described it as atrocious. This route begins just right of a TINY snowpatch, not above a long one. If you are standing under a big snowfield, keep walking back left.

WHERE IT EASES: difficulties relent only on reaching the ridge just south of the true summit, sixteen pitches up. There is no midway escape.

emergency.notes: This is an extremely remote objective. With FSR 8301 and the Lucerne-Holden boat shuttle currently closed/suspended (2026), any rescue would likely require helicopter access; self-rescue capability and a satellite communicator are strongly advised.
emergency.rangerStation: Chelan Ranger District / Wenatchee River Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest
emergency.nearestHospital: Lake Chelan Health Hospital, Chelan, WA (24-hr ER; EMS also stationed in Stehekin)
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Chelan County Sheriff's Office (911 for emergencies)

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails currently inside the fire closure order.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
bivy.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
bivy.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

bivy.name: Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp for the Chelan Mountains crest peaks. From the North Fork Entiat trailhead at roughly 3,880 ft the trail runs about eight miles to the Pyramid trail junction, with Fox Camp a quarter mile north of it. Every one of Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain is reachable from here, which is what makes this the single most useful site here — a party that carries in once can pick off several summits over consecutive days rather than repeating the approach. Saska is the shortest of them, essentially a scramble off the trail near where it crosses the south ridge at Saska Pass; Emerald and Cardinal need the higher basin above. Note this is a different spur road and a different trailhead from the Entiat River trail at the end of the valley, and the two are easy to confuse when planning — turn off roughly 35 miles up rather than driving to the road's end. Season is July through early October, though the larch in late September is the standout. The valley is dry and hot low down and the camp is a genuine relief after it.
bivy.water: The North Fork Entiat River is beside the trail for most of the approach and there is water at the camp. It holds through the season in a normal year. Above Fox Camp the Pyramid trail climbs onto drier ground where water becomes intermittent snowmelt only, so this is the last certain fill for parties going high.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the North Fork Entiat trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The North Fork Entiat River and Pyramid trails are both named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
bivy.capacity: An established backcountry camp with room for a couple of parties; the sites along this trail are described as roomy

approach_variants.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to Chiwawa Basin and the 6,300 ft benches
approach_variants.notes:
Park at Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old mine site. Start up-valley on Buck Creek Trail #1513 for about a mile and a half and BEAR RIGHT at the fork onto Chiwawa River Trail #1550, which takes over an old mining-road grade close to the river — water is reliable along all of this.

About 3.7 more miles brings the signed Red Mountain Trail junction near 4,000 ft. This is the last water that is both obvious and easy to reach before the basin, so fill here. Bear LEFT into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain.

Beyond the junction the tread deteriorates, braids and climbs through forest toward the basin, with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater around 4,400 ft — manageable at summer flow, higher and pushier early. Above the ford the brush thickens and the tread fades: favour the more open, less-timbered ground along the EAST side of the basin, because drifting into the timber turns this into a bushwhack.

Camp is on benches around 6,300 ft. Several lines reach them: the left-trending gully is the most direct and easiest going though it is wet, and the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better choice coming down.

FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, so Trinity is currently not reachable by vehicle.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Sep. The road to Trinity is often not melted out until mid-June, and the upper mountain and col hold snow into July in heavy years
hazards: Misidentifying the gully near the col, which leads to an exposed low-fifth-class dead end
Loose, sandy rock flanking the col and loose talus on the upper mountain
Cornices and early-season snow at the Fortress-Chiwawa col
An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater, and fading braided tread that becomes a bushwhack if you drift into timber
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, so Trinity is currently unreachable by vehicle
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A NOTCH IN SOMEBODY ELSE'S RIDGE, AND SAYING IT THAT WAY IS WHAT MAKES IT FINDABLE: the Fortress-Chiwawa col at about 7,200 ft is the NOTCH IN FORTRESS MOUNTAIN'S EAST RIDGE. From the 6,300 ft benches, traverse steep heather and aim for that notch. You are walking toward a gap on the skyline of the mountain NEXT DOOR, not toward the peak you are climbing.

WHAT THE LAST STRETCH FEELS LIKE, so you know you are on it: the snow slope up to the col is moderate and then steepens noticeably in the final section below the notch, and the rock flanking it is loose and sandy. Stay on the snow or on the most solid line you can find rather than the flanking rock. A slope that stays uniformly moderate all the way to a gap is not this one.

FROM THE COL THE ROUTE HAS NO SINGLE LINE AND THAT IS THE CORRECT ANSWER, NOT A GAP IN THE BETA: work up the south-west side on slabs, gullies and talus taking the path of least resistance. Nothing here is cairned or named.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS EXPLICIT AND IT HAS A STATED CONSEQUENCE: misidentifying the correct gully near the col leads to an exposed low-fifth-class DEAD END. If the ground you are on has stopped offering an easy option and is committing you to fifth-class moves, reverse and pick a different line — this route never needs them.

THE CRUX IS SHORT AND IT IS AT THE TOP: the step gaining the SUMMIT RIDGE is loose and exposed Class 2-3 and is the hardest ground on the route. After it, an easy traverse of about 100 ft to the WEST — to your right — reaches the top. If you gain a ridge and the summit is to your left, you are on the wrong section of crest.

GOING BACK DOWN, USE A DIFFERENT LINE THAN YOU CAME UP FOR ONE STRETCH ONLY: below the benches, the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better descent, and the loose climber's-left skyline gully should be avoided.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek variant to the col west of the summit
approach_variants.notes:
A less-travelled alternative starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead rather than Trinity. It bushwhacks to about 5,500 ft and follows a gully to the right of Point 5971 up to the col WEST of the summit, then takes easy Class 2 ground along the west ridge to the top.

This is the shorter line on paper and the rougher one on the ground: there is no tread on the bushwhack and no camp equivalent to the Chiwawa Basin benches. It is genuinely used, but not recommended over the Trinity approach.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Sep, as for the main line
hazards: An unmaintained bushwhack with no tread from about 5,500 ft and no published landmarks below the gully
No established camp on this side, so it commits you to a long day
Early-season snow in the gully and at the col
Loose rock on the west ridge, as everywhere on this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS VARIANT'S BASE IS A DIFFERENT COL FROM THE MAIN ROUTE'S, AND CONFUSING THE TWO PUTS YOU ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN. The standard line goes to the FORTRESS-CHIWAWA col, which is SOUTH-WEST of the summit and is a notch in Fortress's east ridge. This variant goes to the col WEST of the summit, gained from Phelps Creek by a gully to the RIGHT of Point 5971.

THE TEST IS WHAT LIES ABOVE THE COL YOU REACH. From this one, the WEST RIDGE runs to the summit on easy Class 2 ground — a walk, essentially. From the Fortress-Chiwawa col you face slabs, gullies and talus on the south-west FACE with a loose Class 2-3 step at the top. If you have reached a col and the way on is a broad easy crest, you are on this variant. If it is a face with no obvious line, you are on the standard one.

THE APPROACH MARKER IS A NUMBERED POINT AND THAT IS ALL THERE IS: the gully is to the RIGHT of Point 5971. Nothing else about the bushwhack below it is published, which is why this is the second variant and not the first. Carry a track.

emergency.notes: No cell service in the basin; carry a satellite communicator. Wilderness permits are free and self-issued at trailhead registers (no advance reservation); group size limit is 12 people/stock combined. As of 2026 the Chiwawa River Road is closed by storm damage past Atkinson Flat Campground — verify current road status with the Wenatchee River Ranger District before driving in.
emergency.rangerStation: Wenatchee River Ranger District, Leavenworth — (509) 548-2550 (Chiwawa River Rd/Phelps Creek & Trinity approaches); Chelan Ranger District, Chelan (Holden Village/Railroad Creek approach)
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center, Leavenworth (24/7 ER) is closest for the Phelps Creek/Trinity approach; Lake Chelan Community Hospital, Chelan, is the relevant option for the Holden Village/ferry approach. Both are hours from Cloudy Pass itself — this is a genuinely remote objective.

hazards: CURRENT ACCESS CLOSURE (2026): Holden Village and Forest Service Road 8301 (Lucerne dock to Holden) are closed to all guests under a USFS emergency order following December 2025 flood/landslide damage, with no confirmed reopening as of this writing - the standard boat-and-shuttle approach to this route is not currently usable; verify status with the Chelan Ranger District before planning a trip.
crevasses on the Southeast Glacier/snowfield remnant
loose class 3-4 rock in the ridge-notch gully
exposed, insecure class 4 move below the summit ridge
rockfall
remote, multi-day self-rescue terrain with no cell service
standing dead timber/deadfall in an old burn along the Copper Creek approach trail

watch_out: Six or more creek crossings each way — footing can be slick on wet rock and logs, especially early season.
Less maintained than the standard route; expect more brush and deadfall.
Trail is currently closed under the 2026 Labor Mountain Fire order — verify status before going.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to nonexistent along the Entiat River valley and in the Cow Creek Meadows/Myrtle Lake basin; the nearest reliable signal is generally near the town of Entiat on US-97A. The self-issue wilderness permit left at the trailhead doubles as a basic itinerary record for search and rescue.
emergency.rangerStation: Entiat Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (2108 Entiat Way, Entiat, WA); the district office is closed to walk-ins and calls are currently routed to the Chelan Ranger District, (509) 682-4900.
emergency.nearestHospital: Central Washington Hospital, 1201 S Miller St, Wenatchee, WA — the region's Level III trauma center, roughly 1.5-2 hours by road from the Entiat River Trailhead.

watch_out: The west-side (Buck Creek Pass) option climbs steep, unmaintained grass and heather that is likely dangerous when wet
Use-paths braid above about 5,800 ft with no signage - keep heading uphill and north toward the pass

Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) has been closed beyond Atkinson Flats Campground to Trinity since May 20, 2026 due to storm damage with no reopening estimate - this route may currently be inaccessible by vehicle
itinerary: Day 1: Drive to Trinity Trailhead (road access currently closed - verify before departure) and backpack the ~8.8-mile approach to a camp at Pass No Pass or Buck Creek Pass, both of which have multiple established sites. Day 2: Day-scramble Helmet Butte from camp (1-2 hours round trip from Pass No Pass); many parties combine the outing with nearby Fortress Mountain or Liberty Cap given the shared approach. Break camp and hike partway or fully out. Day 2 or 3: Finish hiking out to the trailhead.

pro_tips: Because the approach is 15-19 miles one-way, most parties combine Carru with Osceola and/or Lago (and often Blackcap, Ptarmigan, and Lost) from a single Shellrock Basin or Eureka Creek camp rather than climbing it alone.
Check Harts Pass Road status with the Methow Valley Ranger District before driving out — the road has a history of storm-damage closures and was closed indefinitely as of spring 2026.
Snow can linger on Freds Pass and Rolo Pass into July; carry an ice axe (and consider microspikes) for an early-season trip.

bivy.name: Cedar Creek meadow camps above the falls
bivy.notes: The western approach camp, and the reason to use this side at all. Cedar Falls comes at about 1.7 miles from the trailhead and is the day-hike turnaround for most visitors; keep going and roughly two miles beyond the falls the trail opens into meadows with good camping. From here the head of the valley and the west flank of North Gardner are within reach, and this is materially shorter than coming round by Wolf Creek. Its real value is seasonal. The trailhead is low and this is one of the first trails in the area to melt out, so in a late spring when Wolf Creek is still buried and the Gardner Meadows approach is a slog, this side goes. The trade is snow higher up and a steeper, less travelled finish. Damage from the 2021 fire is visible in this drainage too, heavier away from the creek than beside it, and the lower trail to the falls is in good order. The trail continues to Abernathy Pass at about 9.2 miles and over into North Creek, which is a useful escape or through-route if weather closes the tops.
bivy.water: Cedar Creek runs alongside for the whole approach and through the meadows, and it is the most dependable water — a snow-fed creek in a north-facing valley that holds well into autumn. Fill here, because the climb east out of the valley toward the Gardner ridge has nothing.
bivy.permit: The Cedar Creek trail is outside the wilderness until it nears Abernathy Pass, where it enters the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No permit or quota either side of that line; party limit of twelve inside. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Campfires prohibited under the forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions and the county burn ban.
bivy.capacity: Good established sites for hikers and stock where the trail enters the meadows; several parties can spread out

bivy.name: Upper Cedar Creek head basin
bivy.notes: A spring and early-summer bivouac rather than a camp, used by parties taking the west side of North Gardner when snow still covers the ground. Getting into the head of the valley involves leaving the maintained trail and working up through brush, and it is not pleasant in dry conditions — the argument for it is precisely that on snow the brush is buried and the travel is fast. From the basin the west and southwest flanks of North Gardner rise directly, and a party can take both Gardner summits and be back at the car the following morning, which is appreciably shorter than the Wolf Creek round trip. Expect avalanche terrain on those slopes into June and treat the timing accordingly: an early start, firm snow, and off the slopes before the afternoon. There is no shelter, the basin is a cold sink, and there is no easy retreat except the way you came. This is a competent-party option in a narrow window, not a general-purpose camp.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and the headwaters of Cedar Creek. Reliable in early season, which is when this camp makes sense; in late summer it thins out and the meadows below the falls become the better choice. Melting snow is the normal answer here in spring.
bivy.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness at the head of the valley. No permit, no quota, party limit of twelve, proper food storage. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions, and there is no fuel. Leave no trace on unestablished ground and camp on rock or snow rather than fragile meadow.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground for one or two small parties; no established sites and no flat obvious platform

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground and the Highway 20 road-head campgrounds
bivy.notes: The obvious place to sleep before starting up either side of the Gardners, and the only one with running water and a toilet. It sits in ponderosa forest just off the highway about four miles beyond Mazama, and the Cedar Creek trailhead is roughly half a mile further along a short forest road — near enough to walk to if you wanted. Coming from the west over the pass, this is the first campground on the dry side and the change is abrupt: open pine, no undergrowth, hot afternoons and cold clear nights. Use it as staging, not as a destination. The practical value is that it lets you drive out the evening before, sleep at the trailhead, and start the long Wolf Creek or Cedar Creek walk at dawn rather than in the heat of the day, which on these approaches matters more than it sounds. Bear in mind the highway itself opened late in 2026 after repair work, and paving through this corridor has been closing individual sites for stretches of a week or so at a time; ring ahead rather than arriving on spec.
bivy.water: Piped water at Klipchuck when the season's system is turned on, and Early Winters Creek nearby. Do not count on the tap outside the main season or in a drought year — check before you drive out, because the alternative is hauling water from town.
bivy.permit: Nightly campground fee. Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for the trailhead lots. No wilderness permit required. Campfires are prohibited under the forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions currently in force, including in established rings, and the county burn ban applies as well. Some highway-corridor sites are closed in rotation for paving work between early August and mid September.
bivy.capacity: Around forty sites at Klipchuck; the smaller campgrounds up and down the highway corridor add a few dozen more between them

watch_out: Holden Village approach is closed as of 2026 — plan on the Phelps Creek/Spider Gap approach instead
Spider Gap glacier travel: moats and crevasses, ice axe required

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails currently inside the fire closure order.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground
